Our proposed system, called botnet IP address group detection (BIGD), leverages
a deep understanding of botnets and their behavior to identify relationships among
IP addresses through the analysis of honeypot command records.
The BIGD method is divided into two primary stages: IP address group formation
and command-based learning, which utilize natural language processing techniques.
In the first phase, word embeddings are utilized to identify clusters of related IP
addresses based on their shared command usage patterns, and then the clusters are
further analyzed in the second phase using machine learning algorithms to classify
them as either legitimate or malicious IP groups.
Our experimental results, using a dataset derived from the Zeus botnet, show that
the BIGD method outperforms other conventional methods, achieving a true positive
rate of 0.99 and a false positive rate of 0.1 in detecting malicious IP address groups.

command data, making it less susceptible to the evolution of botnet behaviors.

Statistical models that utilize tree structures are prevalent across various fields due to their ability to effectively represent intricate relationships. A key challenge in employing tree-based models lies in determining the most optimal tree configuration and associated parameters. In practice, multiple models that share a common parameter space may be evaluated simultaneously to mitigate the issue of overfitting. This paper introduces an innovative method for assessing the performance of tree-based models, which involves analyzing the individual components of tree nodes and then aggregating the results to determine the most suitable model. This approach hinges on a novel statistical test that compares the predictive accuracy of a specific model against a collection of sub-models and super-models. Moreover, we propose a strategy for selecting relevant nodes that contribute significantly to the overall performance of the model. Extensive simulations and a comparative analysis of multiple models for predicting gene expression levels demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed testing framework and node selection procedure. Our method is further validated using real-world data from the GTEx project. Ultimately, this research contributes to the development of a framework for comprehensively evaluating tree-based models, thereby enhancing their practical applications. Our proposed method is publicly available on the R Software Package for Statistical Computing. This package can be accessed at https://github.com/raminagha/mEST. For additional information and supporting materials, please visit https://github.com/raminagha/mEST. Finally, we apply our proposed framework to investigate the relationships among various gene expression datasets within the GTEx network. This thesis introduces a groundbreaking approach to visual object recognition within complex document images, combining the principles of layout analysis and object detection to identify and extract objects from diverse image backgrounds. A novel method for object representation, utilizing a bag of visual word model in both spatial and spatial-temporal contexts, facilitates the classification of retrieved objects, with our system capable of accurately extracting objects from dense, overlapping, and distorted data with high degrees of robustness and accuracy. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in various document image datasets, surpassing the performance of existing state-of-the-art techniques under similar conditions. Furthermore, the versatility of our system is demonstrated through its successful application in two real-world commercial scenarios, the identification of payment slips and checks, with impressive results that are competitive with or even superior to those achieved by human experts. A cutting-edge approach to film restoration is based on a sophisticated model that captures the nuances of film degradation over time. This model involves a complex process where high-quality, high-definition images are progressively degraded and transformed into a lower-resolution format. This process generates noise and artefacts that can be accurately replicated using a statistical approach. However, the current method for applying this model, known as backward transmission, is time-consuming and inefficient due to the need to process all subsequent frames in chronological order. This paper proposes a new method called forward transmission, which enables the model to start generating and refining the degraded images from the beginning, greatly reducing its computational cost. The results show that forward transmission produces comparable outcomes to backward transmission, but with significant improvements in speed and performance. Additionally, the authors demonstrate that forward transmission can be further optimized by using a more efficient method of noise estimation, known as gradient forward transmission. This optimization yields even better results, showcasing the effectiveness of the proposed forward transmission approach in film restoration and its potential applications in a range of other image and video processing tasks. The emergence of deep learning technology has led to growing concerns about intellectual property rights, as it is becoming increasingly difficult to identify and prove ownership of a dataset used to train models that produce similar results. To protect dataset ownership, we propose an innovative approach that incorporates a hidden backdoor signal into data records without compromising their integrity. This strategy, called untargeted backdoor marking (UBM), aims to identify dataset owners by analyzing data characteristics that are not crucial for model performance, making it difficult to detect without significant computational resources. UBM is a novel copyright protection method that prioritizes data owner verification over model performance preservation. To our knowledge, UBM is the first technique capable of preserving data integrity by introducing a hidden signal into data records. Through rigorous testing, we have demonstrated the feasibility of UBM and its potential to identify dataset owners accurately while maintaining data quality. Notably, our results show that UBM performs comparably to existing methods in copyright protection, maintaining data quality and requiring a relatively low amount of computational resources. Moreover, UBM outperforms existing methods in terms of data quality and computational efficiency, making it a promising solution for dataset protection. Notably, our results show that UBM is particularly effective in identifying owners of datasets with high utility, making it a valuable tool for data owners. To facilitate future research, we have released a dataset and made our implementation publicly available. This research marks an important step towards the development of a robust dataset protection framework, addressing the need to identify dataset owners effectively and efficiently. To our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive study on the use of hidden backdoors in dataset protection, making UBM a pioneering approach in this field. While UBM has the potential to be used in malicious contexts, such as attacks on deep learning models, we have focused on its use in dataset protection and copyright protection, where it has shown significant value. This research highlights the importance of a robust dataset protection framework, capable of identifying deep learning models trained on private data, and discusses the potential applications of such a framework, including data protection and copyright protection. Recent breakthroughs in neural abstractive summarization models have made significant progress, but they often generate factually inaccurate summaries. These errors can originate from two sources: first, the models' inherent propensity for making mistakes; second, the differences between their training data and the reference summaries they are modeled after. Our solution to the first issue is straightforward, but we also need to address the second one. Our key insight is that the best way to prevent errors is to rely on the truth, so we have developed a loss function called LoyalSum that rewards models for staying true to fact, rather than mimicking their references. Our experiments show that LoyalSum outperforms the best current models in summarization accuracy and produces fewer factually inaccurate summaries. The Semantic Web has successfully implemented the RDF model using SPARQL, which supports various domains, especially visual information. Nevertheless, the current query language falls short of addressing visual aspects, as it focuses on structured data. To bridge this gap, we propose a new language, VGStore, which integrates visual features into the existing SPARQL framework. VGStore enhances the existing language by providing new pathways to answer visual questions, such as identifying objects and relationships based on attributes like color and texture. Moreover, it introduces a novel data type, visual property, which captures characteristics of objects, such as color and texture. As a result, the new language offers a broader range of capabilities, making it an effective tool for both scene understanding and visual analysis. In this regard, we have developed a new language, VGStore, which leverages the power of the RDF graph and visual information, enabling the creation of a comprehensive visual property graph. Rubin's Galaxies are a pair of galaxies observed in detail through the 1975 Hubble Space Telescope's imaging of the Rubin's Galaxy pair. A machine learning model has been trained to forecast the UGC 2885 galaxy's spectrum using its optical image and the Hubble Space Telescope's imaging as input. A supervised learning approach, employing the K-Nearest Neighbor method with k=5, has been utilized to achieve this. As a result, the predicted spectrum of the UGC 2885 galaxy has been generated, which aligns well with the observed spectrum from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 16. Furthermore, the predicted spectrum exhibits a notable discrepancy from the forecasted spectrum of the UGC 2879 galaxy, which is another member of the Rubin's Galaxies pair. It is hypothesized that the UGC 2889 galaxy may be in the process of undergoing a tidal disruption, which could be attributed to the presence of the gravitational influence exerted by the UGC 2885 galaxy. This hypothesis is further supported by the UGC 2885 galaxy's notable asymmetry in its ionized gas distribution. This finding is significant and could have far-reaching implications for the study of the ongoing interactions within the Rubin's Galaxies system. A detailed analysis of the predicted spectrum of the UGC 2885 galaxy is presented in this study. This research has been submitted to the Astrophysical Journal. Mobile AR applications generate a range of diverse output, including real-time graphics, video, and 3D sound. These can be processed in various ways, such as through software or hardware, and are often created using multiple parallel and sequential services. A novel LSTM-based system for AR service disaggregation has been developed to optimize the use of mobile devices' resources. This system leverages historical data on device performance and AR service requirements to forecast resource allocation, reducing the time required for output generation. In contrast to existing methods, this system can handle sequential dependencies between services and accounts for device resource fluctuations. We evaluated our system against multiple baselines using a large dataset from an augmented reality gaming company, demonstrating its ability to outperform existing methods in terms of output quality and processing time. Specifically, our system achieved an average 12% increase in output quality and reduced processing time by 7% compared to the best baseline. We also identified areas for further improvement and explored potential future research directions. Cache side-channel attacks have been a significant threat to software systems for years, compromising both software and hardware. While previous research has investigated hardware cache side-channel attacks, there is still a knowledge gap regarding software cache side-channel attacks. This study addresses this knowledge gap by introducing CacheQL, a novel language for identifying and analyzing cache side-channel attacks. CacheQL's effectiveness is demonstrated through a comprehensive ground-truth dataset of 12 applications, where it accurately detects cache side-channel attacks in 100% of cases. Additionally, CacheQL is shown to accurately trace the source of these vulnerabilities to specific lines of code in software. An evaluation of 12 production software libraries and APIs using CacheQL revealed that 11 of them, including Apache Commons Math3 and Google Guava, leak sensitive information due to cache side-channel vulnerabilities. Furthermore, CacheQL successfully identified the vulnerable lines of code in these libraries, which in some cases matched the locations identified by previous research. This study's results indicate that CacheQL is a powerful tool for identifying and locating cache side-channel vulnerabilities in software systems. Stable training of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult issue to resolve. GANs are typically classified into two main categories, namely non-saturated and saturated models, which are often associated with the phenomenon of mode collapse. While some researchers attribute mode collapse to issues within the generator, others link it to problems in the discriminator. This paper presents a new perspective on mode collapse, arguing that it is primarily caused by the characteristics of the discriminator's loss function. By analyzing the relationship between the discriminative capacity of the discriminator's parameters and mode collapse, we demonstrate that a lower discriminative capacity tends to result in mode collapse. Through numerical experiments, we assess the effectiveness of the mode regularizer, LiR, in improving mode collapse. Additionally, we examine the relationship between the LiR parameter and the discriminative capacity using Hessian eigenvalues. As a result, we conclude that LiR effectively increases the discriminative capacity of the discriminator's parameters, thereby reducing mode collapse. Moreover, we find that LiR has a positive impact on the stability of the WGAN critic's parameters, leading to more stable training. These findings suggest that LiR enhances both the discriminative capacity and stability of the discriminator's parameters, ultimately preventing mode collapse. This research provides new insights into the mechanisms behind LiR's effectiveness in improving GAN training. Moreover, it highlights the importance of the discriminability of the discriminator's parameters in preventing mode collapse. By doing so, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of the LiR algorithm and its application in GAN training. Furthermore, it underscores the significance of the discriminability of the discriminator's parameters in improving GAN training. By analyzing the Hessian eigenvalues of the WGAN critic's parameters, we can also assess their stability. While this research focuses on the WGAN critic, we believe that this approach can be easily adapted to other types of GANs and GAN critics. In fact, we have successfully applied this approach to the MMD-GAN critic, and the results are promising. In response, we have developed a new method called MultiSAGE, which aims to improve the accuracy of inter-layer connection prediction by incorporating prior information and addressing certain assumptions. MultiSAGE employs a two-stage approach that first learns essential features from individual network layers and then uses these features to identify potential inter-layer connections. The method also allows for the incorporation of prior knowledge related to inter-layer connections. Through experiments on various multiplex networks, we have found that MultiSAGE significantly outperforms existing approaches in accurately predicting inter-layer connections. Additionally, the method successfully recovers hidden inter-layer connections using prior knowledge. Furthermore, the learned layer embeddings and inter-layer connections can be utilized to infer missing connections in real-world networks. Overall, the results demonstrate that MultiSAGE provides a powerful tool for the effective analysis of complex multiplex networks. In our research, we investigate how teams of oscillators interact in a coordinated manner. We propose a unique model that captures the dynamics of these interactions, taking into account team members' unique parameters, internal connections, and external influences. Our results indicate that teams can reach a synchronized state, despite these factors, provided that the parameters are not excessively mismatched and the team is not overly fragmented. Interestingly, teams exposed to the same external signal tend to synchronize more easily than those without one. Moreover, teams with more direct, within-group connections can achieve greater synchrony than those with fewer within-group links. Our findings are supported by case studies using the Kuramoto model, which demonstrate the relationship between connection strengths and synchrony within teams. These results have implications for understanding the coordination of teams in various domains, including social sciences, biology, and economics. Ultimately, our research highlights the importance of considering multiple factors when assessing team coordination, including parameters, internal connections, and external influences. This research investigates the initial stability of spacetimes governed by Einstein's equations, focusing on cases where spacetime evolves from an initial condition near a FLRW geometry with a negative spatial curvature. Employing a long wavelength approximation and perturbative methods, we analyze the stability of these spacetimes during their initial evolution. Our findings indicate that, under certain conditions related to the curvature of the spatial section and the energy conditions in the matter it contains, a cosmic censorship principle holds. Conversely, if the spatial section has too great a curvature, this censorship is compromised, even under conditions that are locally admissible from the matter's perspective. These results provide insights into the initial stability of these spacetimes and reveal how their curvature affects their evolution and our understanding of cosmic censorship. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these findings to the initial evolution of a universe resulting from the collision of two big bang bang universes. Our research also explores the emergence of singularities in these spacetimes and their spatial properties. Additionally, we examine the stability of these spacetimes and the cosmic censorship principle under conditions that violate the null energy condition, revealing a more intricate relationship between curvature and the evolution of spacetime. We explore the properties of a new cubic spline estimator, specifically designed for functions with sharp or near discontinuous derivatives. These functions, often encountered in applications like income data analysis, pose significant challenges to cubic spline estimation. The key issue is that traditional methods may overestimate when faced with steep function edges. To address this, we develop an alternative estimator that maintains its monotonicity while still approximating the function's behavior. The proposed estimator's convergence properties are investigated, and under specific conditions, it is shown to be as efficient as its traditional counterpart. To accommodate the complexity of monotone cubic splines, an objective function's optimization is made computationally more manageable through an iterative approach and efficient subproblem solutions. The proposed estimator's performance is evaluated using a simulated example and an application involving Swiss life satisfaction data analysis. The findings suggest that the proposed method outperforms existing alternatives in terms of accuracy. Additionally, a web-based application is made available for further analysis and exploration. https://www.math.colosse.com/en/colosse/visualisation.html#steep-spline-estimation. To overcome this limitation, we developed a two-step training approach, first fine-tuning CLIP on a small dataset and then utilizing domain-specific prompts to achieve high-quality image-text matching capabilities in unseen areas. This involves creating prompts that are representative of a specific domain and incorporating them into the fine-tuning process, which we call Domain Prompt Learning. Our method allows for seamless adaptation to any new domain, and we have demonstrated its effectiveness by achieving superior performance in domains outside the initial training data. Notably, we observed consistent improvements across multiple evaluation datasets and domains. Moreover, we found that our approach not only enhances performance in unfamiliar environments but also reduces the need for large training datasets within known domains. The effectiveness of image haze removal is often evaluated based on the clarity of details in the original image. However, this approach has a limitation as it prioritizes visual clarity over other considerations, such as image authenticity and texture. This focus has led to the development of new evaluation metrics that take into account different aspects of haze removal, including visual noise and texture. Nevertheless, these metrics still rely on reference images and cannot be applied to cases where reference images are not available. This limitation highlights the need for haze removal evaluation that does not rely on these reference images. To address this gap, a new metric is proposed that does not require a reference image and can capture the subjective experience of image haze removal. This metric is based on the idea that people's perception of haze removal is influenced by the level of haze, as well as the clarity and texture of details in the image. To quantify this experience, a partial divergence-based metric is used, which is then combined with other metrics to develop a comprehensive haze removal evaluation metric that can capture the full range of subjective experiences. This proposed metric is evaluated against existing metrics that require reference images and shows promising results in reflecting the subjective perception of haze removal. Additionally, a public dataset of subjective evaluations is made available to support further research in this area. The final metric is also shown to be effective in evaluating the quality of different haze removal algorithms. The proposed metric is available for download at the following link: https://github.com/zhuyunlin1996/DHQ. Deep learning models have become highly susceptible to attacks that manipulate their inputs to produce desired outcomes. To address this issue, we introduce a groundbreaking technique known as neural payload insertion. This innovative approach involves embedding malicious payloads into deep learning models' internal representations. To achieve this, we develop a novel method called DeepPayload, a tool that allows attackers to exploit any black-box DL model without requiring access to the model's architecture or training data. DeepPayload employs a pre-trained generative adversarial network to generate stealthy payloads that are difficult to detect. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DeepPayload in launching successful attacks against various black-box DL models across different application areas, such as image recognition and language translation. Notably, we found that even the most advanced defensive mechanisms, including adversarial training and ensembles, are ineffective against DeepPayload's attacks. Furthermore, we discovered that embedding payloads that are similar to legitimate inputs improves DeepPayload's attack performance. To assess the security of DL models against DeepPayload, we propose a novel metric called payload transferability, which measures a model's ability to withstand payload insertion. Our analysis reveals that certain defensive mechanisms, such as adversarial training and ensembles, significantly enhance a model's resistance to DeepPayload's attacks. Finally, we discuss the implications of neural payload insertion on the security of DL models and discuss potential countermeasures. This paper introduces a novel approach for 3D object localization through an array code that utilizes a coded assessment technique. By embedding a set of unique codes within the transmit signal, we enable simultaneous channel estimation and object location detection via passive reception, eliminating the need for a dedicated receiver. Our focus is on developing a transmitter consisting of an antenna array and a digital signal processor that can decode the object's 3D position from the received signals. To achieve this, we formulate a problem that maximizes the object's orientational root mean square error (RMSE) while optimizing the code and transmitter design. Our theoretical analysis and simulation results demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, known as Coded Assessment, for achieving precise 3D localization with a single transmitter. Moreover, we investigate the potential for Coded Assessment to be integrated with other techniques, such as beamforming, to further enhance its performance. Our numerical results confirm that a hybrid combination of beamforming and Coded Assessment can significantly improve localization accuracy, with a 40% reduction in 3D localization error at a 1-meter RMSE. Our work provides a foundation for the development of a unified framework for object localization through a single transmitter. Additionally, we introduce a new concept for joint beamforming and coded assessment, which we demonstrate through a practical example using a 5G communication system. Our results indicate that a 5G system equipped with this approach can achieve a 3D localization error of 0.1 meters, 0.3 meters, and 0.4 meters at a 1-meter, 0.5-meter, and 1.5-meter RMSE, respectively, using a single transmitter. This achievement is made possible by leveraging the unique properties of 5G's advanced modulation and signal processing capabilities. Our theoretical and numerical analyses confirm the potential of this approach, underscoring its feasibility and practicality. To facilitate future research, we provide a detailed description of our simulation setup and code. Our contributions to the field of object localization through a single transmitter are expected to stimulate innovative research and advancements in this rapidly evolving field. This research, however, delves into the realm of non-semantic characteristics, such as groupings of data by random labels or patterns of noise embedded in images. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach yields adversarial patterns that are remarkably similar in appearance to the original images, thus underscoring the potential dangers of adversarial patterns based on non-semantic features. This research sheds new light on the potential vulnerabilities of DNNs and highlights the need for robust adversarial defense strategies. An alternative approach, using unalterable data, can offer a simpler and more efficient solution, but its implementation is hindered by the need for specialized equipment that can accurately detect even minute changes in data, a challenge known as the ultra-sensitive detection problem. In this study, we describe an innovative technique for ultra-sensitive detection that can accurately identify alterations to data while also enabling the authentication of its original sender, without the requirement for public key encryption. This method leverages a unique combination of a pseudorandom noise generator and a pseudo-noise detector, both of which can be easily integrated into a single hardware device. A thorough theoretical analysis confirms the robustness of our proposal against various types of attacks. Furthermore, numerical simulations demonstrate its ability to accurately identify even extremely minor changes in data, down to a single photon, a level that far surpasses the sensitivity threshold of current state-of-the-art hardware-based detection systems. With its compact design and exceptional sensitivity, this technique has significant potential to provide an uncomplicated and highly secure communication solution that can be widely implemented. This approach enables the network to efficiently handle small voxel sizes and achieves superior performance on various 3D tasks such as classification, segmentation, and registration. However, these networks expose users to potential security threats from neighboring networks that may have access to their transmitted data. In an attempt to mitigate this risk, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes emitter selection to address this issue. In this approach, we allow only a subset of base stations to transmit data while keeping the remaining stations inactive. By doing so, we minimize the risk of unauthorized data exposure to neighboring networks. Our goal is to identify the most effective subset of base stations that maximizes the security of primary users' data transmission while ensuring a predetermined level of quality of service and confidentiality for secondary users' data reception. To achieve this objective, we formulate an optimization problem that seeks to maximize the overall transmission rate of primary users while minimizing the interference caused to secondary users. The goal of this research is to identify the essential characteristics of learnable images that can be successfully classified using a given neural network. Our approach involves creating an artificial, adversarial version of an image that cannot be classified by a classifier, serving as a measure of the image's learnability. We've developed a comprehensive framework that not only quantitatively assesses learnability, but also provides insights into the image's inherent properties. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework accurately identifies key features of learnable images, such as their presence of textures, simple background colors, and clear labels, even when those features are absent or distorted. Moreover, this framework enables the modification of images to enhance their learnability, offering valuable guidance for image preprocessing and enhancing. Our results demonstrate that this guidance can significantly improve the image's learnability, as validated by human experts. Our research also explores the relationship between adversarial images and natural noise, revealing that both types of perturbations can be used to quantify learnability. Our findings suggest that these perturbations are not only effective for adversarial attacks, but also provide a robust measure of learnability, with the added benefit of being resistant to various types of noise. Our research has the potential to significantly impact the field of image preprocessing and enhancement.

This paper introduces a novel multi-image steganography technique, known as SABMIS, which employs a unified sparse representation to embed multiple images into a single cover image. By minimizing the $l_0$-norm of a sparse coefficient vector, the combined image is obtained, which is then embedded into a cover image using a modified least significant bit substitution technique. The extraction process involves the decomposition of cover data into a sparse representation, followed by image reconstruction. By analyzing the characteristics of sparse representation, the hidden images are successfully recovered. Experimental results demonstrate that SABMIS exhibits superior performance in comparison to standard steganography, as it accommodates multiple images and achieves higher capacity while maintaining a higher peak signal-to-noise ratio. Moreover, the proposed method is resistant to various types of attacks, as it does not require any prior knowledge of cover data. Consequently, SABMIS is considered a blind multi-image steganography technique. An extended version of SABMIS, which incorporates the use of sparse coding dictionaries, is also presented, as the SABMIS-SR variant. Experimental results confirm that SABMIS-SR outperforms SABMIS in terms of capacity and PSNR. The source code of SABMIS and SABMIS-SR is available online. To achieve their missions, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) must be able to identify and track humans within their environment. This ability is crucial for tasks such as disaster response, but current technology falls short of meeting this need. This study presents a novel bio-inspired visual system for UAVs that can recognize humans in real-world settings and learn to make new detections without the need for extensive training. By incorporating a neural system inspired by the human brain, this system can track and distinguish individuals within its scope. Compared to existing approaches, this method outperforms them in terms of both accuracy and speed, making it suitable for use in various practical applications. Furthermore, this system can be implemented on a single NVIDIA GPU in under 30 milliseconds per frame, making it viable for real-time operations. The primary modes of HIV and hepatitis C virus transmission are free virus dissemination and cell-to-cell transfer, although the relative importance of these pathways has not been thoroughly explored. In the case of HCV, determining these contributions is particularly challenging due to the virus's prolonged incubation period, making retrospective studies difficult, and the lack of suitable in vitro models that capture both transmission pathways. To address this, researchers have developed an agent-based model that simulates HUVEC cell cultures infected with HCV, allowing them to quantify the contributions of free virus and cell-to-cell transfer to the spread of the virus within the culture. Using this model, they found that cell-to-cell transfer is the primary driver of HCV spread within the culture, accounting for approximately 80% of new infections, and its effectiveness is influenced by factors such as the activation state of nearby cells, virus load, and the distribution of infected cells within the culture. This study's findings demonstrate the significance of cell-to-cell transfer in facilitating persistent HCV spread, and the model provides valuable insights for the design of antiviral therapies. Moreover, the framework established in this study can be applied to other viral infections, such as HIV, and may reveal novel targets for the development of more effective therapies. Energy system models heavily rely on detailed time-series data to accurately forecast demand and resource availability. By applying this method, the authors demonstrate that it's possible to produce accurate outcomes using time-series data spanning just 5-10% of the original resolution. When compared to a baseline method that uses a 5-day time-series resolution, the new approach produces nearly identical results, but at significantly lower computational costs. Ultimately, this research aims to empower the development of more efficient and accurate planning models that can be scaled up to larger, more challenging problems. Deep neural network-based systems have been widely adopted in autonomous driving applications, particularly in locating and mapping the surroundings. However, existing methods often suffer from low efficiency and poor generalization in location recognition tasks. This is because they process 3D point clouds in a fixed manner, ignoring the inherent structure and distribution of point clouds. To address this issue, we present AttDLNet, an innovative system that leverages attention-driven mechanisms to enhance the processing efficiency and effectiveness of 3D point clouds. By exploiting the inherent structure and distribution of point clouds, our system learns to selectively focus on key features and eliminate noisy ones, leading to improved performance and robustness. We evaluate AttDLNet in a challenging 3D location recognition task, demonstrating its superiority over existing methods through comprehensive experiments. Additionally, our code is available for public access to facilitate further research. 

System Overview: The AttDLNet system consists of three key components, namely an attention module, a distance-aware module, and a cross-view fusion module. The attention module identifies the most informative point clouds by focusing on key features and eliminating noisy ones, while the distance-aware module learns to represent point clouds based on their spatial relationships. The cross-view fusion module effectively integrates the cross-view information to improve the localization accuracy. 

System Pipeline: The overall workflow of AttDLNet is as follows. First, the point clouds are selectively extracted by the attention module, while the distance-aware module processes the remaining points. Next, the two resulting representations are cross-view fused to generate the final output. 

Experimental Results: The overall accuracy of AttDLNet is 85.5%, surpassing the state-of-the-art method, R2DDNN, by a significant margin of 9.2%.

Link prediction is a crucial component of many real-world applications, including knowledge graph completion, recommender systems, and event evolution modeling. However, existing approaches face significant limitations due to the inherent sparsity and temporal nature of evolving graphs. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel temporal graph connection learning framework, GC2LF, capable of effectively capturing both local and long-term dependencies in evolving graphs. GC2LF achieves this by integrating two key modules: a generalized connection network and a semantic correlation recognition component. The GCN component learns to represent generalized connections between nodes, while the SCRC module identifies meaningful correlations between the predicted and existing edges. To enhance the model's temporal awareness, we incorporate a self-supervised transformer transformer to model the temporal dependencies between nodes. Experimental results on link forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches. Notably, our model successfully predicts links on a large-scale, real-world graph of 1.9M nodes and 7.3M edges spanning 10 years. We derive efficient action bounds for the hyperplane partitioning the unit ball and use these findings to investigate the asymptotic behavior of the functional as its arguments converge. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to examine the finite-sum case and explore the consequences for empirical estimation, demonstrating consistency and root-$n$ asymptotic normality under specified moment constraints. The presented concentration results are pivotal in establishing the statistical consistency of our proposed method. Interestingly, our approach enables action minimization without directly solving an associated optimization problem, offering significant computational advantages. We validate the efficacy of our estimator with supporting numerical experiments. The research in this paper is pioneering in its exploration of concentration inequalities for Radon measures within the context of the concave Blaschke-Santorini functional and related finite-sample results. The findings have broader implications for studying the geometric properties of data, facilitating new insights into its structure. Moreover, our estimation results have the potential to be adapted to related estimation problems. This study introduces a novel, stable constraint solver for multi-body dynamics simulations. Building upon the augmented Lagrangian approach, our method leverages the sparse Cholesky decomposition of the Hessian matrix, enabling efficient, first-order solvers that maintain stability. Experimental evaluations reveal that our solver excels in terms of speed and robustness compared to established Newton-based methods. Notably, its ability to withstand numerical instabilities also makes it a reliable choice for complex simulations involving rigid and flexible multi-body structures. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we have applied our solver to a set of benchmark tests, including a virtual launch of the Space Shuttle and a simulation of a flexible spacecraft recovering from an off-nominal deployment of a solar panel. Furthermore, we have also developed a performance benchmark that assesses the solver's efficiency in simulating large-scale, flexible multi-body systems. This benchmark allows us to compare the scalability and efficiency of our solver with other approaches. The code implementing our solver is publicly available on our project's website. To facilitate future research, we have also provided a software interface for solving linear systems using the Cholesky factorization technique. This interface can be easily integrated into various constraint solvers, enabling researchers to leverage the benefits of our solver. The associated software is available for download at https://github.com/ist-sfheimbruck/Cholesky. When tested on real-world data from a CO2 storage site, our approach outperformed existing methods, with an average error rate of just 0.0004 s. Our findings suggest that this technology has the potential to revolutionize CO2 storage monitoring, enabling near real-time monitoring across multiple sensors. By making this technology more accessible, we hope to facilitate widespread adoption and inform best practices for reducing greenhouse gas emissions worldwide. To our knowledge, this is the first in-situ implementation of a CNN-based CO2 monitoring system, with the code and model available for public use. We believe that this breakthrough will pave the way for more affordable and efficient CO2 monitoring across diverse settings. In a Federated Learning (FL) system, vehicles with similar internet connections exchange data to update a shared neural network model, but this approach is impractical for edge networks due to limited battery power and high vehicle movement, leading to connectivity disruptions. To address this issue, we developed a new framework called Vehicular Edge Federated Learning (VEFL), which optimizes data exchange, minimizes vehicle movement, and ensures model convergence even with poor connections. By creating a network of connected vehicles, VEFL forms clusters to reduce the data required for model updates, but this requires carefully selecting vehicle groups to prevent convergence issues caused by similar model updates. To tackle this challenge, we employed a two-stage clustering approach, first identifying clusters, and then selecting the most effective ones. Extensive testing of real-world datasets revealed that our VEFL approach significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of convergence, energy efficiency, and communication costs. Notably, VEFL demonstrates up to 99.5% convergence rates, reduces energy consumption by 90%, and minimizes communication costs by 99%. Furthermore, VEFL showcases strong scalability by achieving 0.0004 F1 scores on the CLEVR color, shape, and size classification task with 1000 vehicles, compared to 0.0006 scores of the best existing method. The study will reveal the practical benefits of VEFL in autonomous driving edge networks, leading to improved energy efficiency and reduced communication costs. By applying VEFL to autonomous driving edge networks, we can achieve significant energy and communication savings, paving the way for its adoption in other mobile edge networks. The research also discusses the broader implications of this work in the context of document image analysis and explores its potential to support various tasks, such as document retrieval and image understanding. Recent research has exposed significant vulnerabilities in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) by introducing adversarial disturbances into their parameters, allowing for undetectable manipulation of their internal architectures, which can be exploited to trigger targeted misclassifications. This study delves into the feasibility of utilizing such adversarial disturbances to embed backdoors into DNNs, revealing that the two methods are mutually exclusive due to the requirement of backdoored models to maintain their original functionality. Through a combination of theoretical analysis and empirical testing, we have established that parameter tampering is not a viable method for embedding neural backdoors. This finding has significant implications for the development of robust and trustworthy AI systems, underscoring the necessity for the research community to adopt more stringent evaluation criteria for AI reliability. A pairing of vertices within a graph $G$ is known as a perfect matching if every vertex in $G$ is paired exactly once, excluding any additional edges. Given a graph $G$, a specific type of perfect matching $\pi$ can be identified by a one-to-one mapping of its vertices, such that each edge in $\pi$ shares a common vertex with exactly one other edge not in $\pi$. This matching is known as a $\pi$-flawless pair, and pairs in $\pi$ are referred to as $\pi$-flawless pairs. This paper aims to explore the computational complexity of finding a perfect matching $\pi$ that contains a specified number of $\pi$-flawless pairs within a graph $G$ under certain restrictions on its vertices. It is known that this problem is NP-complete for general graphs, but when the graph's vertices are colored in a specific way, a more efficient algorithm can be employed. This algorithm can find a perfect matching that contains exactly $k$ $\pi$-flawless pairs within a graph $G$ with $O(kn + \sigma(G))$ time, where $G$ has a specified coloring and $\sigma(G)$ represents the size of its matching edge set. Furthermore, this algorithm can be modified to find a perfect matching that contains exactly $k$ $\pi$-flawless pairs and satisfies a specific condition on the degrees of its vertices within a time complexity of $O(kn + m)$. This condition is known as the total degree constraint, where each vertex must have a specified degree $t$ and the algorithm can find a perfect matching containing exactly $k$ $\pi$-flawless pairs within that constraint. However, this algorithm cannot be modified to find a perfect matching containing exactly $k$ $\pi$-flawless pairs and satisfying the total degree constraint in general cases. This approach enables the generation of all possible translations, which can then be filtered to ensure they conform to the language's grammatical rules. In this work, we derive a tractable approximation for the partition function of a certain class of models known as Graph Attention Tokenization networks, which are a type of Graph Attention Network that builds upon the conventional Graph Attention Network by introducing a splitting operation. GATs dependent on this operation are more computationally resource-intensive but can process larger datasets, making them highly appealing. However, the computational cost associated with deriving exact solutions for these networks poses a significant challenge, prompting us to propose a more efficient solution. We develop a variational approach that approximates the partition function of these networks, which can be used to obtain an accurate and tractable approximation of the true partition function. This new approach enables the approximation of a wide range of network structures, including those with varying attention heads and edges, without the need for additional modifications. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed solution by testing it on a series of benchmark datasets, including the ZINB model, yielding promising results. Moreover, the proposed approach is computationally efficient and can be easily integrated into existing machine learning pipelines. This work paves the way for further research into estimating the partition function of these networks, which can have a significant impact on the field of machine learning. Polariton chemistry, an emerging field, leverages strong interactions between light and molecular matter to facilitate novel chemical reactions driven by collective behavior. However, theoretical ab initio modeling of these interactions is challenging due to the complex quantum nature of polaritons. This study addresses the difficulties encountered when simulating polaritonic chemistry ab initio. By examining the influence of non-equilibrium steady states and quantum collectivity, we aim to shed light on the subject matter. To achieve this, we employ a simplified model consisting of a molecule coupled to a cavity and driven by an external laser field. Our results demonstrate that the model exhibits a unique self-sustaining steady state characterized by a distinct quantum collectivity. Furthermore, we investigate the model's behavior in the presence of a cavity-molecule coupling and find that the system is capable of inducing a non-equilibrium state characterized by a non-thermal molecular population, which is also non-thermal in its absorption and emission of energy. Our findings suggest that the interaction between non-equilibrium steady states and quantum collectivity is crucial for the success of polaritonic chemistry. Additionally, we discuss the limitations of the current ab initio methods and propose a strategy to overcome these challenges. This study serves as a foundation for the development of a quantum theory for polaritonic chemistry ab initio. Ultimately, our long-term goal is to provide a comprehensive framework for ab initio modeling of polaritonic chemistry. This study represents an initial step towards this ambitious objective. Future research will focus on the theoretical and computational development of a quantum theory for polaritonic chemistry, which will be a key area of research at the Max-Planck Institute for Nuclear Physics in 2023. Finally, we will address the limitations of current data-driven modeling approaches and propose new directions for research. We believe that the insights presented in this paper will be helpful to researchers and policy makers as they continue to navigate the COVID-19 pandemic and prepare for potential future epidemics. We investigate the influence of the prior probability distribution on the maximum likelihood estimate of the parameters in a family of probability distributions, specifically focusing on how small changes in parameters affect the estimates. Through a case study of Ising models, we examine the estimates' continuity and show that changing the prior probability distribution causes the estimated parameters to converge to a set of values under certain conditions. Additionally, our analysis reveals a connection between the convergence of the empirical covariance matrices of the estimates and the spectral properties of the Hessian matrix of the logarithmic likelihood, providing a geometric explanation for the convergence. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the estimated parameters exhibit asymptotic dependence on the parameters being estimated and the configuration space, leading to the conclusion that the estimated parameters are not necessarily consistent in general. Instead, their convergence depends on the parameters, specifically the inverse of the covariance matrix, as we prove in a general framework. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate the practicality of our findings. Specifically, our research shows that the convergence of the estimated parameters depends on the size of the lattice and configuration space, and that the convergence rate can be controlled by these factors. Finally, our results indicate that the estimated parameters may not necessarily converge to their true values, but rather converge to a set of values that we term the asymptotic parameter space, which we define and investigate in depth. This type of malicious activation exploit allows malicious models to produce incorrect results when presented with a specific trigger. Research has shown that backdoors can be easily inserted into models, and when trained on compromised datasets containing a small number of backdoored samples, they can lead to catastrophic failures in real-world applications. Given the stealthy nature of these attacks, individuals may lose confidence in facial recognition and avoid its use, thus undermining the privacy rights of those who rely on facial recognition systems. To mitigate this issue, we investigate the effects of backdoors on face recognition and propose a novel defense mechanism called Backdoor- and Adversarially-Resistant Face Recognition (BAAFear). Recent advancements in real-time semantic segmentation using deep learning have seen significant progress, but traditional CNN-based methods still face limitations due to their reliance on convolution for extracting local features, which can be ineffective for recognizing semantic objects with complex shapes. In contrast, Transformers have demonstrated impressive performance in vision tasks, but their high computational cost makes them unsuitable for real-time applications. Our solution, the RTFormer, leverages a novel efficient architecture that combines the strengths of CNN and Transformers for real-time segmentation. This model features a novel transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture with a multi-scale design, which integrates CNN and Transformer components for real-time segmentation. Our results show that the RTFormer outperforms state-of-the-art real-time methods in terms of accuracy, speed, and IOU metrics on various benchmark datasets, with a inference speed of 68.5 FPS. This paper delves into the visual characteristics of neural networks and explores the potential of color as a means to visually convey complex network behavior through an abstract representation.  The goal is to develop a method for creating color palettes that accurately reflect the performance of neural networks in a specific task, and to use these colors as an intuitive means of interpreting the network's internal workings.  The study begins by analyzing the fundamental principles of color and developing a mathematical framework for creating distinct, human-distinguishable hues.  A computational approach is introduced, based on a mathematical model of color perception, to produce a range of visually distinct colors in high quality.  The paper then describes a novel method for creating color palettes that accurately represent the dynamics of neural networks, and provides an initial demonstration of this technique in action.  Finally, the study concludes by identifying potential future challenges and opportunities for applying color-based visual analysis to the field of machine learning.  A companion technical report providing additional details is available online.

We explore the properties of the Hamiltonian dynamics in three cosmological models with two degrees of freedom that are classified as superintegrable. These models are distinguished by their respective Hamiltonian expressions: a second-order, a first-order with constant coefficients, and a first-order with arbitrary coefficients. A key observation is that the first two models exhibit symmetries in their Hamiltonian expressions, whereas the third does not. This distinction prompts an examination of the interrelation between variational invariance and superintegrability. Specifically, we identify a link between these two concepts in the context of Lagrangian dynamics, namely that variational invariance is a prerequisite but not a guarantee of superintegrability. This relationship is further illustrated by analyzing the first-order cosmological model, which is found to be variational invariant but not symmetric under Noether's principle, and subsequently demonstrating that its Hamiltonian dynamics is nonetheless superintegrable. This conclusion is supported by the derivation of three additional conserved quantities for the model, which are in addition to the three known conserved quantities associated with the first-order model. A similar analysis is performed for the first-order cosmological model, which is found to be non-symmetrical and consequently not variational. This analysis yields a single unknown arbitrary function and two unknown arbitrary coefficients, which can be freely specified. Interestingly, we observe that the simplest of these three models, namely the second-order cosmological model, is the only one that remains fully determined after imposing the principle of Noether invariance. This is in contrast to the first-order models, which require specification of their respective arbitrary functions and coefficients. This distinction is further highlighted by the derivation of an additional conserved quantity for the non-symmetrical first-order model, which can be expressed in terms of the arbitrary function and coefficients. This finding underscores the significance of variational invariance in the context of superintegrability. Finally, we extend our analysis to a cosmological model with two degrees of freedom and a third-order Hamiltonian expression. In this study, we examine a stochastic contextual multi-armed bandit problem where multiple options are available with varying costs across different contexts. The key assumption is that when only two options are considered, the more expensive option always has precedence, based on an underlying ordering relationship in the context. We develop two novel algorithms, Contextual Ordered UCB and Ordered Thomas Cover, that take into account this ordering information to yield improved performance compared to existing bandit algorithms. Under certain conditions, these algorithms achieve a regret of $O(d\sqrt{t}\log(t))$ for push and $O(d\sqrt{t}\log(t))$ for pull, where $d$ is the number of relevant context dimensions. Notably, this represents a $O(\log(t))$ improvement over standard bandit algorithms and demonstrates that contextual ordering information can lead to substantially reduced regret. The applicability of our results extends to contextual bandit problems, such as online learning in auctions. We further investigate the scenario where the ordering relationship is unknown, developing a framework for regret analysis and providing an algorithm with regret bounds of $O(d\sqrt{t}\log(t))$. Deep learning inference has become a major bottleneck in edge and cloud systems, 
resulting in increased energy consumption and memory demands for complex models. 
To address this issue, this paper introduces AppealNet, a cutting-edge cooperative 
framework that optimizes DNN inference by efficiently utilizing edge and cloud 
resources. AppealNet's innovative offline and online partitioning approach 
consists of two phases: initially, it divides tasks between edge and cloud nodes 
based on model characteristics, then dynamically adjusts to optimize runtime based 
on performance and resource usage. We evaluate AppealNet's effectiveness using 
NVIDIA's Tegra and Intel's SkyLake processors, demonstrating significant speedups 
for models like ResNet-50 and MobileNet-1.5 on edge devices, with corresponding 
improvements in energy efficiency and latency. AppealNet's approach also enables 
cooperative inference for larger models like ResNet-101, with substantial 
performance enhancements on cloud servers. Overall, AppealNet achieves a 2x speedup 
on edge devices and up to 10x on cloud servers, with energy efficiency improvements 
up to 20x and 80x respectively. AppealNet's results are comparable to or even 
superior to state-of-the-art solutions, with average accuracy gains of 0.8% and 
0.6% respectively. AppealNet's open-source code is available on GitHub.

Numerical case studies are conducted to illustrate the application of the model to optimize ground transportation systems. This research aims to facilitate decision-making for airport operators, transportation providers, and travelers, and can be adapted to address congestion issues in other complex transportation hubs, such as seaports or shopping centers. Ultimately, the findings of this study can empower travelers to make more informed choices and contribute to reducing overall traffic congestion. They are now being re-examined within a shared framework of Borel data structures and a revised proof has been developed, revealing an unexpected connection between these theorems and their ability to be interchanged. This newfound understanding sheds light on the expressive power of Borel data, providing new insights into the relationship between these theorems. Furthermore, this work lays the groundwork for the application of Borel data in the study of polynomial time problems, a related area of research. A novel numerical technique is proposed for a stochastic model of neural stimulation, where moments of the activity of neurons within a population are calculated over time. This approach simplifies complex equations by only accounting for the mean and variance, making it more computationally efficient than traditional methods. Well-posedness of the resulting system of differential equations is demonstrated, and numerical experiments are performed to evaluate the performance of the new method. Compared to a well-established alternative, the proposed method exhibits superior accuracy and efficiency while avoiding the numerical instability that often plagues traditional methods. Furthermore, the new method is shown to be particularly effective when dealing with weak noise conditions. Additionally, the proposed method's ability to accurately capture the dynamics of neural networks is demonstrated through the study of coupled neural oscillators, highlighting its potential for use in various applications. The development of this method is seen as a promising step towards creating a more efficient neural model. All related codes have been made publicly available for further use and exploration. Further research is needed to expand this method's applicability and optimize its performance in more complex scenarios. Our proposed approach, Asset Reassignment, offers an innovative solution for 
trimming networks by repositioning specific nodes. Asset Reassignment relies 
on a thorough understanding of node roles and network requirements to 
intelligently trim underperforming nodes while preserving those with vital 
functions. In contrast to the existing network trimming technique (NTrim), 
Asset Reassignment allows for the flexible assignment of nodes to assets, 
enabling it to trim more effectively by considering a wider range of nodes. 
Furthermore, our findings demonstrate Asset Reassignment's ability to outpace 
NTrim in terms of network resilience and resource allocation efficiency. The 
practical application of Asset Reassignment has been successfully implemented 
in a case study involving the Fortum DSO network, with the tool accessible 
through https://github.com/alan2203/asset_reassignment. Building on this concept, 
our team has also developed a more advanced method, trimmed network trimming 
(TNT), which enhances the existing network trimming technique by repositioning 
nodes to enhance network resilience. However, this new method is not yet 
available for public use. For more detailed results, including the case study 
and TNT implementation, please refer to the corresponding technical report. 
A video demonstrating TNT is available at https://youtu.be/7s5qYXzjKQY. 
Additionally, TNT's source code can be found at https://github.com/fortum/dsorc/branch/tnt.

In quantum systems with time-varying robust interactions, we developed an approach to diagonalization, which effectively addresses the challenge of time dependence in exact diagonalization methods. This issue arises because the Hamiltonian's eigenvectors change at each time step in systems with time-varying robust interactions. Our method employs perturbation theory to address this problem, focusing on the system's nearest perturbative terms. It generates a sequence of diagonalization solutions, which ensures that the system's diagonalized matrix elements remain accurate to the desired order of perturbation at each time step. This approach is versatile and applicable to any quantum system with robust interactions, regardless of whether it's in a ground or excited state, and it can be applied to both finite and infinite systems. Furthermore, we tested this method in a specific example and found that the system's diagonalized matrix elements match the exact diagonalization method to a high order of perturbation. This approach offers a practical solution to a critical problem in quantum systems with time-varying robust interactions. We investigate the behavior of quantum Markov chains with dynamic transition rules applied to limited state spaces that are affected by time-dependent loss of quantum coherence. The quantum operations in this model are restricted to a limited state space without any upper limit on the number of states. The model is inspired by the findings of research on quantum computing algorithms, which suggest that using such a strategy could significantly reduce the required number of states, thus improving performance. The proposed model is based on a mathematical representation of quantum operations as dynamic quantum operations. This representation is used to derive an equation describing the behavior of the model over time, which we call the limited state dynamic quantum master equation. We analyze the properties of this equation and demonstrate that its solution can be used to describe the behavior of quantum Markov chains with time-dependent transition rules applied to limited state spaces. Furthermore, we show that the solutions to this equation can be used to estimate the accuracy of quantum operations in the model and to compare the performance of different quantum operations. We also investigate the impact of time-dependent decoherence on the performance of quantum operations in the model and demonstrate that using decoherence, rather than ignoring it, can lead to improved performance. Finally, we present numerical simulations of the model and demonstrate its potential applications in the context of quantum computing. The proposed model is particularly relevant to systems with limited state spaces, such as quantum computing systems, and could also be applied to other quantum systems with similar properties. account for time-varying factors and correlations between different time points. To

weighting of temporal factors and extraction of key patterns from the data. By
merging bilinearity and temporal attention, LRTA demonstrates improved performance in
predicting time-series data, such as commodity price forecasts, and exhibits robustness
under noisy and sparse conditions. The model's effectiveness is further highlighted
by its low computational and memory requirements. A detailed analysis of LRTA reveals

Our approach involves formulating an optimization problem with an objective function representing the state of convergence, and using it to determine key geometric characteristics of the convergence process. Utilizing this method, we investigate the convergence properties of several preconditioned iterative solvers and compare their performance in both normal and modified modes of operation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of this method by applying it to a real-world application: assessing the convergence rates of preconditioned iterative solvers for an $axially\-symmetric$ Helmholtz equation. This solution is crucial in the context of ultrasonic phased arrays used in industrial inspection and medical imaging. Our findings show that the preconditioned eigenvalue solvers with the Conjugate Gradient method can achieve high convergence rates, surpassing those of unpreconditioned alternatives while maintaining stability. Additionally, we examine the influence of the preconditioning strategy on solver performance and identify the necessity of a tailored preconditioner for optimal efficiency. Moreover, we demonstrate that the proposed gradient descent approach can be adapted for use as a diagnostic tool within the iterative solvers themselves, enabling real-time monitoring of the convergence process and facilitating early termination or aborting the solver. This real-time monitoring can be seamlessly integrated into production systems, yielding significant benefits in terms of computational efficiency and reduced energy consumption. Ultimately, we envision that the proposed approach can be widely applicable to a broad range of eigenvalue problems and iterative solvers. A key active learning technique for training sequence classification models is
to evaluate unlabelled sequences using question selection methods that guide
the training process, but this approach is often hindered by limited label
availability and high annotation costs, a constraint present across both
active and traditional learning methods. To address this challenge, we've
developed a novel method that boosts the effectiveness of active learning by
improving the overall quality of unlabelled training data. We achieve this by
leveraging a model's own predictions to refine its own performance, which in turn
improves the sequence assessment function's accuracy. This process enables more
informative assessments, driving active learning to extract the most valuable and
relevant information from the training data. We've rigorously tested this
approach on multiple sequence classification tasks and observed notable
improvements in the performance of the active learning process, often leading to
notable increases in the accuracy of the model's predictions. We've also found
that this approach is particularly beneficial in scenarios where the quality of
the initial data is poor, where it consistently outperforms other methods. The
implementation of our approach is available for public review.

Specifically, Self-Managed IoT consists of three key components: a personal edge server that enables users to create and manage their own edge servers using their personal devices, a personal cloud server that processes computations offloaded from personal edge servers, and a self-management system that optimizes resource and energy efficiency by offloading computations between personal devices and edge servers. This study introduces a framework that automatically measures heart rates during intense physical activities, such as fitness videos, using the pre-existing data from wearable devices like smartwatches. Our approach first detects the start of these videos, inferring the wearer's pulse rate at that point, based on their documented physical characteristics and a stated pulse rate. We then identifies the segments where the participant's pulse rate remains relatively stable, allowing for a more precise measurement. A novel feature extraction method called "Pulse Rate Magnets" is utilized to create a model that can predict the actual pulse rate with the aid of a regression algorithm. Our framework is tested on 40 fitness videos and achieves an average accuracy rate of 14.4 beats per minute, with a success rate of 61% when the pulse rate range is between 100-120 beats per minute. We also conduct a qualitative evaluation by comparing our system's results with the pulse rate data from a fitness tracker worn by the participant, demonstrating its efficacy in everyday scenarios. Our findings show that it is feasible to develop a smartwatch-free system that can estimate a person's heart rate during intense physical activities, using a pre-existing data-driven approach. This paper presents a novel approach to Tunisian Arabizi speech transcription, a task that poses significant challenges due to the language's complex morphology and phonetics. Specifically, it tackles the issues of diacritics, proper nouns, and unique word formations in Arabizi transcription. To address these complexities, we introduce a multi-task sequence forecasting framework that leverages multi-gram information to generate transcription sequences. This involves three key tasks: predicting the next sequence of characters, determining the next character in a word, and identifying unique word formations. Our proposed system is trained on a large dataset of Tunisian Arabizi speech and utilized to evaluate several diacritization rules. Furthermore, we release a comprehensive dataset of 1,500 minutes of Tunisian Arabizi speech and 2,000 hours of corresponding acoustic features. This dataset is made publicly available to promote further research in this area. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed system outperforms competing methods, achieving an accuracy of 85.3% on the test set. Our results also reveal that our proposed diacritization rules outperform existing rules with an accuracy of 92.7%. This research paper explores statistical compressed sensing techniques for reconstructing three-dimensional images from mixtures of Gaussians. The primary goal is to develop a reconstruction method that can accurately identify and quantify the individual components within a blended image, even when the total number of components exceeds the available measurement frequency. To achieve this, we propose a Bayesian approach that utilizes a hierarchical model to estimate the parameters of each component, assuming that the underlying components are drawn from a known distribution. The Bayesian estimator is then derived using Gibbs sampling, and its performance is evaluated through simulations on various image datasets. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach in recovering the individual components, especially when the components are dissimilar, although it may struggle with convergence in complex scenarios involving a large number of components. To address this limitation, we introduce an alternative method that combines nonparametric clustering with a hierarchical Gaussian mixture model, accompanied by an efficient optimization algorithm for real-time implementation on 3D point clouds. The results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach over existing methods in terms of accuracy and speed. The accompanying video further illustrates the efficacy of the proposed method in real-world applications involving 3D scans of human faces and indoor environments. Ultimately, this research serves as a starting point for exploring compressed sensing techniques in the context of 3D image reconstruction and analysis. Deep learning-based semantic segmentation for aerial images has seen significant advancements. However, existing approaches neglect the dynamic nature of aerial images, which results in poor performance when applying pre-trained models to new images. This limitation stems from a lack of consideration for the changes in image appearance due to factors like illumination, viewpoint, and object transformations. To overcome this, we introduce a new framework known as DIAL, which incorporates a dynamic and context-aware approach to aerial image semantic segmentation. This involves incorporating a module that captures semantic relationships between objects, as well as another that encodes a semantic-aware latent representation. We demonstrate that DAIL outperforms existing methods in multiple aerial image benchmarks, including semantic segmentation, and provide a detailed analysis of its components to show their individual contributions. Furthermore, our framework's adaptability is demonstrated by successfully transferring it to a new domain with limited labeled data available. This work is the first to consider the dynamic aspects of aerial image semantic segmentation, and its dynamic and engaged learning mechanisms can also be applied to other computer vision tasks. This approach falls short when dealing with dynamic environments where time is of essence. To tackle this challenge, researchers have developed Temporal Change Reinforcement Learning (TCRL), a novel method that takes into account temporal variations in the environment. This innovative approach allows agents to adapt to changing conditions over time. In this context, the term 'change' encompasses both the environment's dynamic nature and the emergence of new information. TCRL tackles this dual challenge by incorporating a temporal change metric and a temporal memory mechanism. This unique approach enables agents to learn from past experiences and apply them to future situations, thereby navigating complex temporal environments effectively. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of TCRL through its successful deployment in three distinct applications: (1) learning to navigate a robot in a dynamic environment, (2) optimizing resource allocation in a temporal setting, and (3) detecting anomalies in time-series data. The results of these experiments showcase TCRL's superior performance compared to established benchmarks. This pioneering work opens up new avenues for RL in the context of temporal change. To this end, nonlinear differential-algebraic equation models are being developed to simulate energy grids, considering the interconnectedness of power, heat, and refrigeration systems, along with renewable energy sources. However, these models are inherently nonlinear and non-differentiable, rendering traditional state estimation methods ineffective. To address this limitation, a new framework is proposed, leveraging the structure of DAEs to construct a state transition matrix, thus enabling the use of established estimation techniques. The framework is further demonstrated to be computationally efficient and applicable to both continuous-time and discrete-time models. A key application of this approach lies in assessing the operational status of energy grids, including determining anomalies and potential control actions for system correction. The framework is also shown to be robust in the presence of noisy data and uncertain systems, thus offering a reliable tool for energy management. To validate its effectiveness, a case study is presented, simulating a district heating system, and successfully recovering system states from noisy data. The findings are expected to contribute significantly to the development of advanced management systems for emerging energy infrastructure.
